weeks.title: Establish the baseline
weeks.goal: Practice steadily this week. (1)

study.title: Trace one RAG request
study.detail: Run AnomalyOps and follow one question from retrieval through the final answer. Mark every step you cannot explain without notes.
study.doneWhen: A short request-flow sketch names the actual functions and the gaps to review.

study.title: Practice task 2
study.detail: List each technical claim and reported metric on your current resume. Link each to its implementation, experiment, or work example.
study.doneWhen: Every claim has an evidence link or an explicit needs-verification label.

build.title: Run the existing baseline
build.detail: Start the application and its current evaluation with the documented commands. Preserve errors and results before changing code.
build.doneWhen: The command, environment notes, and actual output are recorded, including any blocker.

build.title: Try an independent API change
build.detail: Attempt one small endpoint validation change using documentation and no generated implementation. This is a diagnostic, so stop at the time limit and record where you got stuck.
build.doneWhen: The attempt and specific gaps are recorded; completion is not required for the diagnostic.

weeks.checkpoint: You can show this week's work. (3)

weeks.title: Understand retrieval
weeks.goal: Practice steadily this week. (4)

study.title: Read the retrieval path
study.detail: Trace chunk creation, embedding generation, storage, similarity search, and top-k selection in your own code. Identify the actual embedding provider, model, and similarity measure.
study.doneWhen: You can explain the pipeline and its configuration without guessing or relying on a generic RAG diagram.

study.title: Audit Hit@5 and MRR
study.detail: Calculate Hit@5 and MRR manually for a small example, then inspect the denominators and relevant-document labels in your evaluation. Investigate the reported embedding-dimension change.
study.doneWhen: You can derive both metrics and explain exactly which data and configurations produced your reported numbers.

build.title: Reproduce retrieval results
build.detail: Run the same retrieval cases against the documented configurations. Record changes to embeddings, indexes, or data that prevent a fair comparison.
build.doneWhen: A reproducible comparison includes actual results and explicitly identifies any number that cannot be reproduced.

build.title: Test one retrieval change
build.detail: Change one variable, such as chunk overlap or top-k, and compare the same development cases. Keep the change only if the evidence supports it.
build.doneWhen: One small experiment has a hypothesis, before-and-after results, and a keep-or-revert decision.

weeks.checkpoint: Explain a failed retrieval example, one design tradeoff, and each resume retrieval metric without notes.

weeks.title: Defend tool calling
weeks.goal: Understand exactly how the model requests tools and how your application controls execution.

study.title: Trace every existing tool
study.detail: Follow the schema, argument parsing, execution, result handling, and next model step for each tool. Distinguish a model request from an authorized application action.
study.doneWhen: You can trace one successful call per tool and identify which code performs each safety check.

study.title: Explain failure boundaries
study.detail: Inspect stopping rules, timeouts, invalid arguments, tool errors, and run consistency. State what each guardrail actually prevents and what remains possible.
study.doneWhen: A short failure table links each risk to an implemented control or an acknowledged gap.

build.title: Exercise rejected tool calls
build.detail: Create small cases for invalid arguments, an unsupported tool, and a failed dependency. Use the real execution boundary rather than only calling a validation helper.
build.doneWhen: Each case produces an observable, understandable failure without an unintended side effect.

build.title: Fix one tool weakness
build.detail: Implement the highest-value missing validation or error-handling behavior. Add a focused regression check for the failure it addresses.
build.doneWhen: You can demonstrate the original failure, the fix, and the behavior that remains unsupported.

weeks.checkpoint: Explain all four existing tools, one rejected request, one dependency failure, and why a bounded tool workflow differs from an unrestricted agent.

weeks.title: Make evaluation credible
weeks.goal: Separate retrieval, answer, citation, and tool quality so the evaluation score has a defensible meaning.

study.title: Inspect every existing case
study.detail: Read the current evaluation questions, expected evidence, scoring rules, and outputs. Check which cases were used during development and whether the overall score mixes different denominators.
study.doneWhen: Every current case has a purpose and every reported aggregate can be traced to its component results.

study.title: Define useful failure labels
study.detail: Create concise definitions for retrieval misses, unsupported answers, bad citations, tool errors, and correct abstentions. Review ambiguous cases manually.
study.doneWhen: You can consistently label sample successes and failures and explain the limitations of any automatic judge.

build.title: Improve evaluation output
build.detail: Make the existing runner expose per-case outcomes and the evidence needed to inspect a failure. Preserve reproducible inputs and configuration.
build.doneWhen: A failed case can be diagnosed from the recorded result rather than only an overall percentage.

build.title: Add focused failure cases
build.detail: Add a small set of carefully reviewed cases for absent evidence, misleading citations, and tool failure. Reserve them as development cases rather than presenting them as untouched test data.
build.doneWhen: The new cases exercise meaningful failures and the baseline is rerun with the changed denominator clearly stated.

weeks.checkpoint: Reproduce the current score and explain what it does and does not establish. Correct unsupported resume wording now.

weeks.title: Audit the anomaly model
weeks.goal: Defend the model, features, split, and limitations behind your anomaly-detection claims.

study.title: Trace data into predictions
study.detail: Follow raw sensor data through feature windows, labels, training, and inference. Explain the Random Forest choice and the most important features in your actual implementation.
study.doneWhen: You can explain one complete prediction and distinguish training-time work from request-time work.

study.title: Check leakage and metrics
study.detail: Audit split construction for related samples or overlapping windows crossing boundaries. Compare accuracy with precision, recall, class balance, and an appropriate simple baseline.
study.doneWhen: You can defend the split or identify the change needed, and explain why synthetic-data accuracy is limited evidence.

build.title: Reproduce the model result
build.detail: Run the documented training and evaluation process. Save split rules, configuration, confusion counts, and the baseline needed to interpret the score.
build.doneWhen: The result is reproducible or a specific reproducibility blocker is documented without substituting a guessed number.

build.title: Fix the largest evidence gap
build.detail: Address one concrete issue found in the audit, such as a leakage-prone split, missing baseline, or incomplete inference documentation. Compare results honestly if the score falls.
build.doneWhen: You can explain it without notes. (5)

weeks.checkpoint: Explain the model's baseline, likely false-positive cost, split rules, and real-world limitations in five minutes.

weeks.title: Own the backend
weeks.goal: Show that you can work on the API, database, and development environment independently.

study.title: Read API and database boundaries
study.detail: Trace request validation, dependencies, sessions, transactions, queries, and response models in your backend. Identify how a failed request affects database state.
study.doneWhen: You can trace one read and one write, including a rollback or error path.

study.title: Review professional work examples
study.detail: Work through this step and note what you can't yet explain. (6)
study.doneWhen: You have two specific contribution stories with your role, a technical decision, verification, and a limitation.

build.title: Make an independent backend change
build.detail: Implement a small validated API/database feature using documentation but no generated implementation. Exercise both success and failure paths.
build.doneWhen: The change works, persists or reads data correctly, and has a meaningful check for its main failure mode.

build.title: Rebuild from a clean setup
build.detail: Follow the repository setup in a fresh environment or container. Fix missing steps and deliberately diagnose one safe configuration failure.
build.doneWhen: Another developer could reproduce the setup without your shell history or undisclosed local files.

weeks.checkpoint: You can implement a small backend change and debug a setup problem without handing the implementation to an AI assistant.

weeks.title: Pass the resume defense
weeks.goal: Complete the first full project defense by November 18, then close the largest remaining ownership gap.

study.title: Give a recorded project defense
study.detail: Explain AnomalyOps for 20 minutes without a script: architecture, retrieval, tools, evaluation, tradeoffs, failures, and your contribution. Include where AI assisted and how you verified it.
study.doneWhen: The recording is reviewed and vague or unsupported answers become a short ranked gap list.

study.title: Recheck the weakest explanation
study.detail: Use the actual code and primary documentation to repair the highest-priority gap from the defense. Explain it again from memory afterward.
study.doneWhen: The revised explanation includes implementation details, one failure case, and an honest limit.

build.title: Close one ownership gap
build.detail: Make the small code or evaluation change that best resolves the defense gap. Avoid unrelated refactoring or a new feature backlog.
build.doneWhen: The changed behavior is demonstrable and linked to the gap that justified the work.

build.title: Package reproducible evidence
build.detail: Create a concise project walkthrough with setup commands, evaluation commands, representative outputs, architecture, and limitations.
build.doneWhen: A reviewer can run the project and verify the central claims from repository instructions.

weeks.checkpoint: You can show this week's work. (7)

weeks.title: Secure boundaries and bound failures
weeks.goal: Define demo access controls and the Azure path while repairing copilot timeouts, dependency errors and tool recovery.

study.title: Map access and data risks
study.detail: Identify public routes, protected routes, stored data, tool permissions, and secrets. Decide what one signed-in demo user should and should not be able to access.
study.doneWhen: A compact access table states the intended behavior for anonymous, authorized, and unauthorized requests.

study.title: Choose the Azure deployment path
study.detail: Review current official guidance for the smallest suitable Container Apps and database setup. Estimate recurring costs and identify spending alerts and cleanup steps before creating resources.
study.doneWhen: The deployment choice, expected costs, secret locations, and resource-removal steps are written down.

build.title: Implement protected routes
build.detail: Add one consistent authentication path and server-side authorization checks for the demo's protected operations. Keep the permission model narrow.
build.doneWhen: The intended user succeeds while anonymous and unauthorized requests fail predictably.

build.title: Remove unsafe secret handling
build.detail: Move application secrets to the appropriate runtime configuration and inspect logging for accidental disclosure. Document required variable names without including secret values.
build.doneWhen: The app starts from documented configuration and the repository and sample logs contain no exposed credentials.

weeks.checkpoint: The access plan and cloud spending plan are explicit; copilot failure/recovery tests pass or remain visible blockers.

weeks.title: Measure real anomaly events
weeks.goal: Study startup and dependency behavior; implement event-level anomaly metrics and validation-only threshold selection.

study.title: Trace production startup
study.detail: Review the container command, dependency installation, configuration, health checks, database initialization, and migrations. Identify what must survive a restart.
study.doneWhen: You can explain the startup order and distinguish persistent state from temporary container files.

study.title: Design bounded failures
study.detail: Review timeout, retry, and error-reporting behavior for model calls, tools, and database access. Avoid retrying side effects blindly.
study.doneWhen: Each external dependency has an explicit timeout or limit and a defined user-visible failure behavior.

build.title: Verify container and persistence
build.detail: Build the container from a clean checkout and restart it after writing representative data. Fix assumptions that rely on local files or a developer-only environment.
build.doneWhen: The app starts consistently and the intended persistent data survives a container restart.

build.title: Exercise dependency failures
build.detail: Simulate one unavailable model or tool dependency and one database failure safely. Fix the highest-value missing timeout or error response.
build.doneWhen: Requests terminate predictably and useful diagnostics identify the failed dependency without leaking secrets.

weeks.checkpoint: Known event fixtures and threshold-selection tests pass. Do not claim completed deployment from a design review.

weeks.title: Keep a light maintenance week
weeks.goal: Use a reduced load as a planning assumption for possible finals pressure. Move this light week if your actual academic calendar differs.

study.title: Review deployment instructions
study.detail: Read the setup and deployment notes as if you were a new contributor. Identify only blockers to running the current version.
study.doneWhen: The top documentation blockers are listed and ordered by impact.

study.title: Rehearse one technical story
study.detail: Practice a concise explanation of a retrieval or tool failure you diagnosed and fixed. Include the evidence used to choose the fix.
study.doneWhen: You can tell the story in three minutes and answer two follow-up questions.

build.title: Fix one setup blocker
build.detail: Resolve the smallest high-impact setup issue from the documentation review. Keep the change limited to a reproducibility problem.
build.doneWhen: The previously blocked step works when followed exactly as written.

build.title: Preserve a working baseline
build.detail: Run the current core checks and save the known working configuration and revision. Record any remaining deployment blocker for the next full week.
build.doneWhen: A known working revision and its verification results are easy to locate.

weeks.checkpoint: Three hours of main tasks maximum. Academic deadlines take priority; do not create a catch-up backlog for optional work.

weeks.title: Verify configuration in a light week
weeks.goal: Practice steadily this week. (8)

study.title: Check cloud configuration
study.detail: Review the chosen Azure resource settings, deployment permissions, health checks, and database connectivity. Confirm the spending and cleanup plan remains acceptable.
study.doneWhen: Required settings and unresolved account or access blockers are explicit.

study.title: Explain deployment recovery
study.detail: Walk through how you would identify a bad revision, inspect logs, and return to a known working version. Use the actual deployment mechanism.
study.doneWhen: The recovery steps identify concrete commands or controls and the revision to restore.

build.title: Deploy the smallest working version
build.detail: Use the selected deployment path for the existing container. If access or account setup blocks deployment, record the exact blocker and preserve a locally verified release candidate.
build.doneWhen: A cloud endpoint responds or a specific external blocker and verified local candidate are documented.

build.title: Run the first cloud smoke check
build.detail: Check startup, one protected request, one database operation, and logs in the deployed environment. Carry only concrete failures into the next week.
build.doneWhen: The four smoke-check outcomes are recorded, including any checks blocked by deployment access.

weeks.checkpoint: You can show this week's work. (9)

weeks.title: Improve retrieval and diagnose failures
weeks.goal: Improve chunk boundaries, source-path signals and test-file weighting; use available local or cloud traces for operational study.

study.title: Inspect real request logs
study.detail: Follow one request through API handling, retrieval or tools, and model output in the environment that actually runs. Use the local server if cloud publishing is pending and label the evidence local. Identify correlation fields without storing sensitive content.
study.doneWhen: You can reconstruct the successful request and identify missing diagnostic context.

study.title: Review service failure behavior
study.detail: Compare intended timeout, retry, authentication and persistence behavior with available smoke-check results. If cloud publishing is pending, use local failure tests and separately record unverified cloud assumptions. Rank remaining gaps by reviewer impact.
study.doneWhen: A short ranked list links each material failure to an observed result and a proposed fix.

build.title: Close cloud deployment blockers
build.detail: Resolve the highest-priority issues from the first deployment and verify persistent data and protected operations in Azure. Avoid expanding the resource footprint without a demonstrated need.
build.doneWhen: The deployed service passes the core startup, access, and persistence checks or the precise remaining external blocker is reported.

build.title: Add useful request diagnostics
build.detail: Add request correlation, timings, and dependency outcome fields where they are missing. Demonstrate one safely simulated failed request in the deployed environment.
build.doneWhen: Logs explain which step failed and how long it took without exposing secrets or misleadingly reporting success.

weeks.checkpoint: Versioned retrieval comparisons and trace evidence are saved. Local evidence is labeled local; Azure publishing is not assumed complete.

weeks.title: Publish defensible copilot results
weeks.goal: Expand the retrieval evaluation and harden batching/settings/lifecycle while studying measurement and release recovery.

study.title: Interpret latency and usage
study.detail: Define a small representative workload and decide which latency and model-usage numbers are useful. Distinguish sample measurements from production-scale claims.
study.doneWhen: The workload, sample size, measurement method, and limits are stated before reporting results.

study.title: Review release and recovery
study.detail: Inspect which checks run before deployment and how a bad revision is detected and restored. Confirm the documentation matches the current environment.
study.doneWhen: You can explain the complete path from a code change to a verified release and recovery.

build.title: Measure the deployed service
build.detail: Run the defined workload and record observed latency, errors, and model usage. Diagnose the largest issue before considering any optimization.
build.doneWhen: A concise results table includes the exact workload and identifies the main performance limitation.

build.title: Prove deployment is repeatable
build.detail: Release a small safe change using the documented process, verify it, and exercise recovery to a known good revision when practical. Complete any missing CI check tied to a real failure risk.
build.doneWhen: A fresh release and its verification are reproducible, with tested or explicitly untested recovery steps labeled.

weeks.checkpoint: A reviewed evaluation of about 50 cases is the first target, with denominators and failures visible. The former December 31 cloud build milestone is deferred to the January release gate because repair work replaces those build hours.

weeks.title: Benchmark anomaly quality honestly
weeks.goal: Compare rules, normal-only IsolationForest and RF across seeds; study a separate held-out copilot case matrix.

study.title: Design the case matrix
study.detail: Choose case categories that match the application's real use: answerable questions, absent evidence, citation support, tool behavior, and dependency errors. Avoid padding the set with near-duplicate easy questions.
study.doneWhen: A coverage matrix explains the purpose and expected evidence for each category.

study.title: Define the held-out protocol
study.detail: Separate cases used for tuning from cases reserved for the final check. Decide how to report small sample sizes, ambiguous labels, and cases later exposed during debugging.
study.doneWhen: The split and reporting rules prevent development results from being presented as untouched test performance.

build.title: Author reviewed evaluation cases
build.detail: Expand the set using actual source material and tool constraints. Verify expected answers and evidence manually before counting a case.
build.doneWhen: The expanded dataset records source evidence, expected behavior, category, and split for every new case.

build.title: Run and inspect development cases
build.detail: Run the development split, inspect failed and borderline outputs, and correct invalid labels. Keep the reserved split out of iterative tuning.
build.doneWhen: Development results have inspected failure categories and any label corrections are documented.

weeks.checkpoint: Anomaly comparisons use the same event protocol and report mean/spread. Grow the copilot set beyond 50 only when case quality and available time justify it.

weeks.title: Make serving reproducible and testable
weeks.goal: Repair real inference and the raw-window endpoint while practicing evaluation diagnosis and reporting.

study.title: Diagnose the largest failure group
study.detail: Inspect development results to separate retrieval, generation, citation, tool, and operational failures. Select the largest actionable problem rather than the most interesting new feature.
study.doneWhen: A specific failure group has a supported root-cause hypothesis and a bounded proposed change.

study.title: Prepare honest result reporting
study.detail: Review denominators, category scores, judge limitations, and representative failures. Decide which claims the sample can support and which would overstate the evidence.
study.doneWhen: A draft results explanation includes reproducible numbers and meaningful limitations.

build.title: Improve one evaluated behavior
build.detail: Implement the bounded fix, rerun development cases, and check for regressions in other categories. Freeze the candidate before the reserved evaluation.
build.doneWhen: The keep-or-revert decision is supported by development results and a fixed revision is recorded.

build.title: Run the reserved evaluation
build.detail: Finish reviewing the target case set and evaluate the frozen candidate on the held-out split. If results prompt further tuning, label those cases as exposed and reserve fresh cases for a later independent check.
build.doneWhen: The report separates development and held-out results, states the final case count, and includes important failures.

weeks.checkpoint: Inference validation and offline/online equivalence tests pass. Explain the evaluation evidence without claiming unperformed experiments.

weeks.title: Repair storage; study protocols narrowly
weeks.goal: Make storage metadata, transactions and readiness correct. Keep MCP/A2A/framework work conceptual until core repairs pass.

study.title: Understand MCP and A2A
study.detail: Use current primary documentation to compare tool access through MCP with communication between agents through A2A. Trace client, server, schema and permission boundaries in a minimal documented example. Keep this conceptual while portfolio correctness repairs remain; do not claim hands-on deployment.
study.doneWhen: You can explain their different purposes and when your current application does not need A2A.

study.title: Inspect one orchestration framework
study.detail: Choose one framework relevant to the target role and read a minimal tool-workflow example. Compare its state, stopping, and error behavior with your existing implementation.
study.doneWhen: You can name a concrete benefit and cost of adopting it without treating framework use as the goal.

build.title: Wrap an existing tool with MCP
build.detail: Expose one or two existing bounded tools through a small MCP adapter and call them from a client. Preserve input validation and the tool's existing limits.
build.doneWhen: A client completes one successful call and one rejected call, with the adapter code kept small.

build.title: Complete a bounded framework lab
build.detail: Recreate one simple existing tool workflow in the chosen framework as an isolated exercise. Demonstrate a stopping condition and one failure path.
build.doneWhen: The lab runs and a short comparison explains whether the main app would benefit from migration.

weeks.checkpoint: Stored runs reflect actual artifacts and failed loads roll back. Protocol familiarity is described as conceptual unless a working example was actually built.

weeks.title: Pass the core repair and readiness gate
weeks.goal: Verify reproducible deployment, honest portfolio claims and project-defense readiness by January 31.

study.title: Run an independent project review
study.detail: Ask a developer to use the demo and question your architecture, evaluation, and contribution. If no reviewer is available, record the walkthrough and use a concrete review checklist without labeling it an independent review.
study.doneWhen: The review produces observed issues and difficult questions rather than only general praise.

study.title: Assess interview readiness
study.detail: Review recent unfamiliar-problem performance, the independent backend exercise, and the project defense. Identify the two weakest areas to prioritize in February.
study.doneWhen: The readiness assessment cites actual attempts and selects two specific weaknesses with follow-up drills.

build.title: Fix the largest review blocker
build.detail: Address the highest-impact issue preventing a reviewer from using or understanding the project. Keep lower-priority ideas out of the release scope.
build.doneWhen: The reviewer can repeat the affected flow or the original reproduction now passes.

build.title: Publish a defensible project package
build.detail: Finalize concise setup instructions, architecture, evaluation results, deployment notes, limitations, and your contribution. Check that resume and portfolio claims agree with the evidence.
build.doneWhen: The demo, repository instructions, results, and interview explanation tell a consistent, verifiable story.

weeks.checkpoint: Correctness/security gates must pass before optional February TypeScript. Verify authorized/unauthorized access, persistence, failure handling, artifact creation and a reproducible release. If cloud access or implementation remains blocked, record it and use February build time to finish core work; never claim a deployment you did not verify.

weeks.title: Close core gaps; start TypeScript if ready
weeks.goal: Repair the January gaps first. If ready, use the weekend build blocks for JavaScript and TypeScript fundamentals.

study.title: Study the highest-priority gap
study.detail: Choose the weakest area from the readiness review and work through its underlying concept using your code or a small example. Avoid broad review with no demonstrated need.
study.doneWhen: You can explain the missing concept and solve a different small example without notes.

study.title: Define capstone ownership
study.detail: Write down the perception, control, integration, or validation work you personally own and the interfaces you depend on. Coordinate scope with the actual team plan.
study.doneWhen: Your contribution, dependencies, and one measurable success criterion are explicit and accurate.

build.title: TypeScript 1/8: JavaScript and async baseline
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Check these before each block if you deferred the track. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. Do not skip prerequisites or extend the 12-hour budget. If a core gap remains, use this time for the fallback below; do not double the workload. First 30 minutes: implement array/object transforms, a module import/export, and one async request with error handling using docs but no generated solution. If these are unfamiliar, spend this block on the linked JavaScript guide and repeat the exercise. Otherwise spend 20 minutes on the TypeScript intro and 40 minutes converting the exercise with strict checking. Fallback while the core gate is unmet: Repeat the failed skill independently. Attempt a fresh version of the January task that exposed the gap, under a time limit and without generated implementation. Review only after the attempt.
build.doneWhen: A small independently written program runs and you can explain its async success and error paths. If deferred, save the fallback result and the unmet gate.

resources.title: MDN: Using promises
resources.assignment: Use up to 30 minutes for the prerequisite check; practice is part of this block.

resources.title: TypeScript for JavaScript Programmers
resources.assignment: 20-minute orientation only if the JavaScript check passes.

build.title: TypeScript 2/8: model the existing API
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Check these before each block if you deferred the track. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. Do not skip prerequisites or extend the 12-hour budget. If a core gap remains, use this time for the fallback below; do not double the workload. Read Everyday Types for 20 minutes. For 60 minutes, model an existing AnomalyOps request, response, and citation using types or interfaces, arrays, optional fields, and unions. Use 10 minutes to explain inference and strict null checks. Work in the existing repo. Fallback while the core gate is unmet: Capture a capstone baseline. Use existing project work to record one baseline for your own module, such as tracking behavior, latency, or failure handling. Count relevant required capstone work toward this block.
build.doneWhen: The type checker catches a deliberate invalid assignment and your normal example passes. If deferred, save the fallback result and the unmet gate.

resources.title: TypeScript: Everyday Types
resources.assignment: 20 minutes on functions, object types, optional properties, and unions.

weeks.checkpoint: One weak skill has a fresh independent result, and your capstone contribution has a measurable starting point.

weeks.title: Build a typed API client
weeks.goal: Keep backend interview practice during the week; build a small typed AnomalyOps client on the weekend if the core gate is met.

study.title: Review a database failure
study.detail: Study one actual weak point involving transactions, query behavior, constraints, or concurrent requests. Use a small reproducible example rather than memorizing definitions.
study.doneWhen: You can predict the example's behavior and explain how the chosen database constraint or transaction prevents the failure.

study.title: Rehearse API design choices
study.detail: Explain validation, status codes, pagination, retries, and idempotency through one endpoint you might build. Focus on the choices relevant to the endpoint rather than adding every pattern.
study.doneWhen: A ten-minute explanation covers the endpoint's contract, failure behavior, and one design tradeoff.

build.title: TypeScript 3/8: safe runtime boundaries
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Check these before each block if you deferred the track. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. Do not skip prerequisites or extend the 12-hour budget. If a core gap remains, use this time for the fallback below; do not double the workload. Read Narrowing for 20 minutes, then spend 60 minutes parsing an unknown JSON response with small runtime checks. Finish with a 10-minute explanation of why a TypeScript type assertion cannot validate incoming JSON. Fallback while the core gate is unmet: Complete a timed backend exercise. Implement a small endpoint with database access and a meaningful edge case in a scratch exercise. Use documentation but no generated solution during the attempt.
build.doneWhen: A valid payload passes and a malformed payload produces a clear error without unsafe access. If deferred, save the fallback result and the unmet gate.

resources.title: TypeScript: Narrowing
resources.assignment: 20 minutes on typeof checks, discriminated unions, and control flow.

build.title: TypeScript 4/8: one API client
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Check these before each block if you deferred the track. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. Do not skip prerequisites or extend the 12-hour budget. If a core gap remains, use this time for the fallback below; do not double the workload. Build one typed fetch wrapper for an existing read-only endpoint. Handle a non-2xx response, invalid JSON or shape, and a request timeout. Use a mock response if the backend is unavailable. Keep credentials and model API keys on the server. Fallback while the core gate is unmet: Fix one practical weakness. Repair the largest issue from the timed exercise and repeat the affected behavior on a different input. Avoid polishing code that was already sufficient.
build.doneWhen: Demonstrate successful data loading and two failure paths; explain every line without generated code.  If deferred, save the fallback result and the unmet gate.

resources.title: MDN: Using promises
resources.assignment: Reference only when blocked; most of the block is implementation.

weeks.checkpoint: Practical backend performance is improving through measured attempts, not only through framework vocabulary.

weeks.title: Connect one TypeScript screen
weeks.goal: Practice AI service tradeoffs and give your existing project one small, reliable TypeScript interface.

study.title: Design one realistic AI service
study.detail: Walk through requirements, request flow, data boundaries, evaluation, latency, and failure handling for a document assistant or bounded tool service. State assumptions before choosing components.
study.doneWhen: A compact design includes justified choices and the first likely bottleneck.

study.title: Review the weakest design answer
study.detail: Use a recent mock or interview to select one uncertain topic, such as caching, queues, or access control. Study only enough to answer the concrete follow-up correctly.
study.doneWhen: You can answer the follow-up with a simple example and explain when the mechanism is unnecessary.

build.title: TypeScript 5/8: one useful screen
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Check these before each block if you deferred the track. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. Do not skip prerequisites or extend the 12-hour budget. If a core gap remains, use this time for the fallback below; do not double the workload. Spend 75 minutes adding a minimal TypeScript browser screen showing an existing AnomalyOps run summary or retrieval result. Use plain DOM and familiar HTML/CSS to keep scope small. Spend 15 minutes explaining the data flow. No new backend, framework migration, or second product. Fallback while the core gate is unmet: Measure one service tradeoff. Run a bounded experiment on the existing project, such as top-k versus latency or a timeout versus failure rate. Reuse the established evaluation set appropriately.
build.doneWhen: One screen displays real or clearly labeled fixture data from the typed client. If deferred, save the fallback result and the unmet gate.

build.title: TypeScript 6/8: visible failure states
build.detail: Start this track only after the January gate: you can defend RAG/tool/evaluation claims from code, make an independent backend change, and demonstrate the core API/access/evaluation checks. Work through the eight lessons in order; if delayed, do the earliest unfinished lesson within the remaining February slots and record which lesson you actually completed. study.title: Prepare concise technical answers
study.detail: Practice answers to likely follow-ups about embeddings, grounding, tool permissions, evaluation, SQL, and deployment. Use your actual implementation and admit unsupported details.

study.detail: Listen to a recording for unexplained assumptions, rambling, and skipped correctness checks. Choose one communication behavior to change in the next session.

weeks.title: Strengthen debugging under pressure

build.title: Prevent the demonstrated regression
build.detail: Apply the smallest correct fix and add a check that would detect the same meaningful failure. Avoid tests that simply repeat the implementation.

weeks.checkpoint: You can narrate a disciplined debugging process and show one regression prevented by evidence-driven work.

weeks.title: Refresh the candidate story

weeks.checkpoint: Your current materials communicate the strongest verified work without increasing the number of claims you cannot defend.

build.title: Close the most relevant gap

weeks.checkpoint: Preparation supports actual opportunities. New portfolio features stay paused unless they address a demonstrated hiring or project need.

study.title: Explain measurements and limits

weeks.title: Close the strongest opportunities
weeks.goal: Prepare well for active late-stage conversations and make remaining technical claims easy to verify.

study.title: Review open interview questions

build.doneWhen: The attempt is completed and reviewed for the specific criteria the role requires.

build.title: Resolve one sharing blocker
build.detail: Work through this step and note what you can't yet explain. (14)

portfolio.assignment: Read the specific audit IDs listed below. Line numbers refer to the audited revision, not necessarily current code. Record fix/verification evidence in notes.

items.title: Alerts use ground-truth labels to pick the sensor and anomaly type
items.detail:
- **Where:** `alerts.py:229` (`sensor = row['target_sensor']`), `alerts.py:248` and `:281` (`anomaly_type: row['anomaly_type']`), `alert_events.py:67` and `:191` (events grouped by `anomaly_type`), `db_queries.py:95`.
- **What's wrong:** `target_sensor` and `anomaly_type` are generator labels. The model only outputs one machine-level score per row. Every alert is attributed to the sensor the generator corrupted, and every event is labeled with the true anomaly type. In production you would not have either.
- **Evidence:** all 82 false positives land on sensor `"none"` with the "target sensor was not recognized" reason; every true positive is attributed to exactly the right sensor.
- **Why it matters:** the "Sensor Distribution" and "Anomaly Type Distribution" charts, event grouping, and event drill-down are all label leakage. Anyone reviewing the project who reads `alerts.py` will catch this.
- **Fix:** make the model produce what the alert needs. Simplest route: the per-sensor labels `{sensor}_anomaly` already exist in the data, so train one classifier per sensor (or a `MultiOutputClassifier`) and alert on whichever sensor scores above threshold. If you want anomaly type on the dashboard, add a separate multi-class classifier trained on `anomaly_type` and show its prediction, labeled as predicted. Keep `target_sensor`/`anomaly_type` only in an evaluation column (e.g. `true_sensor`, `true_anomaly_type`) that the alert logic never reads. Then group events by `(machine_id, predicted_sensor, step gap)`.

items.title: Hard safety-limit violations are never alerted unless the model also fires
items.detail:
- **Where:** `alerts.py:330-332` (only `prediction == 1` rows are considered), `alerts.py:257` (only the target sensor is checked).
- **What's wrong:** `check_violation` runs only on rows the model flagged, and only on one sensor. A reading above `critical_high` on a row the model scored 0 produces nothing. `ALERT_TYPE_THRESHOLD` (`alerts.py:43`) is defined and never used.
- **Evidence:** 129 sensor readings in the test window exceed a warning or critical limit on rows with `prediction == 0`; 10 more are on non-target sensors of flagged rows. None of them alert.
- **Fix:** run the rule check on every row and every sensor independently of the model. Emit a `threshold_violation` alert when only the rule fires, `model_anomaly` when only the model fires, `model_and_threshold` when both. Rules are the safety net; they must not depend on the model.

items.title: False positives get higher severity than real low-confidence detections
items.detail:
- **Where:** `alerts.py:244` (unknown sensor hardcoded to `SEVERITY_WARNING`), `alerts.py:200-203` (`assign_model_severity` returns `INFO` below 0.70).
- **Evidence:** all 82 false-positive alerts are WARNING; 335 true-positive alerts are INFO. 32 FP events are WARNING.
- **Fix:** goes away once P0-1 is fixed (there is no "unknown sensor" path). Until then, the fallback should be the lowest severity, not WARNING.

items.title: Fresh clone cannot run the pipeline
items.detail:
- **Where:** `generator.py:308` (`save_sensor_data` calls `to_csv` with no `mkdir`), also `features.py:297`, `alerts.py:348`, `alert_events.py` `save_alert_events`.
- **Evidence:** `python generator.py` on a clean checkout raises `OSError` because `outputs/` is gitignored.
- **Fix:** `Path(output_path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` in every save helper (`model.save_dataframe` already does this; reuse it). Add a CI job that runs the pipeline end to end on a small dataset (see P1-9) so this cannot regress.

items.title: Running `pytest` overwrites your real model artifacts with a toy model
items.detail:
- **Where:** `model.py:256-287` writes to the global `ARTIFACT_DIR` regardless of the paths passed in; `tests/test_model.py:168-190` calls `run_model_pipeline` and even reads `artifacts/model_metadata.json` from the repo.
- **Evidence:** after `pytest`, `artifacts/feature_columns.json` contains `["temperature", "temperature_delta"]`. If you trained the real model first, it is gone, and `/predict` silently serves the 2-feature toy.
- **Fix:** add an `artifact_dir` parameter to `run_model_pipeline` and pass `tmp_path` in the test. Same pattern for every module that writes to a hardcoded path.

items.title: `build_features` ignores its own sort
items.detail:
- **Where:** `features.py:20`: `df.sort_values(...).reset_index(drop=True)` result is discarded.
- **Evidence:** feeding the same data shuffled produces different features: 484 of 485 `temperature_delta` values differ.
- **Why it matters:** it only works today because the generator happens to emit rows in step order. Any other input (DB export, real data, `/predict` batch path later) gets garbage features with no error.
- **Fix:** `df = df.sort_values(['machine_id', 'step']).reset_index(drop=True)`. Add a test that shuffles input and asserts identical output.

items.title: `/predict` accepts garbage and calls it an anomaly
items.detail:
- **Where:** `model_serving.py:20-27`, `schemas.py` `PredictionRequest`.
- **What's wrong:** missing features are filled with 0, unknown keys are silently dropped, and there is no size limit. The README (`README.md:460`) documents the zero-fill as intended behavior.
- **Evidence:** `{}` and `{"bogus": 1e9}` both return `prediction: 1, score: 0.83`.
- **Fix:** return 422 if any expected feature is missing or any key is unknown (list them in the error). Reject NaN/inf. Update the README.

items.title: The labels are wrong right after every anomaly ends
items.detail:
- **Where:** `generator.py:285-300`. When `remaining_duration` hits 0 the label flips to normal, but the value is still wherever the spike/drop/drift/impossible_value left it. `step_normal` mean-reverts at 10% per step, so the signal takes roughly 20 to 30 steps to recover while being labeled normal. Clipped `impossible_value` (e.g. voltage 0 becomes 55 on the next step) is the worst case.
- **Evidence:** 100% of test false positives fall in that recovery window.
- **Why it matters:** your false-positive count measures generator artifacts, not model behavior. It also teaches the model that "obviously abnormal value" is sometimes normal.
- **Fix:** pick one and document it. (a) Reset the sensor to a normal value when the anomaly ends. (b) Extend the label through a recovery period until the value is back within the normal band. (c) Keep the labels but exclude a recovery window from scoring and report it separately. (b) is the most realistic.

items.title: Only row-level metrics are reported, and they overstate the alerting quality
items.detail:
- **Where:** `model.py:76-100`, `evaluate.py`.
- **What's wrong:** rows inside one 100-step drift are 100 highly correlated samples. Operators care about events: was the anomaly caught, how fast, how many false events per machine-day.
- **Evidence:** row precision 0.965 vs event precision 0.72.
- **Fix:** add event-level recall (event detected if at least one alert overlaps it), event precision (alert events overlapping no true event), detection latency (steps from true start to first alert, median and p90 by type), and false events per 1000 machine-steps. Report those in the README as the primary numbers. Drop `accuracy`; at a 25% base rate it says nothing.

items.title: The purge gap is justified wrongly and does not cover the real leakage
items.detail:
- **Where:** `config.py:13` (`PURGE_GAP_STEPS = 50`), `README.md:250`.
- **What's wrong:** the README says the gap stops rolling windows crossing split boundaries. The features are backward-looking only, so a validation row using training-period history is not leakage (you would have that history in production). The actual max lookback is 78 steps anyway (train starts at step 79 after `dropna`), so 50 would not cover it even if it mattered. The real risk is a single anomaly event appearing in two splits, and drift/stuck_sensor run up to 100 steps.
- **Evidence:** 2 anomaly events span the entire second purge gap, so the same event is in both validation and test; 13 events touch a purge region.
- **Fix:** set the gap to at least the max anomaly duration (100), or drop any event that crosses a boundary from both sides. Rewrite the README sentence to describe what the gap actually prevents.

items.title: Some anomaly types are trivially detectable by construction
items.detail:
- **Where:** `generator.py` `stuck_sensor` (returns the exact same float every step, so `delta == 0.0` exactly), `impossible_value` (negative pressure/flow or exactly 0 V).
- **Evidence:** recall 1.00 for stuck_sensor, drop, impossible_value.
- **Fix:** add small quantization noise to stuck values (real stuck sensors still jitter at the ADC level) and report per-type results so a reader sees the hard types (spike, drift, oscillation) separately from the easy ones. Headline F1 is inflated by the easy types.

items.title: Generator leaks the label into non-target sensors
items.detail:
- **Where:** `generator.py:260-264`. During any anomaly, every non-target sensor gets extra noise that only exists while `mode == 'ANOMALY'`.
- **Why it matters:** the model can partly learn "machine is in anomaly mode" from sensors that are supposedly normal. Small effect, but it is a pure simulation artifact.
- **Fix:** delete those lines, or apply the same extra noise in normal mode.

items.title: Results come from one seed and one split
items.detail:
- **Where:** `generator.py` `DEFAULT_FIXED_SEED = 295`, `model.py` single train/val/test.
- **Fix:** run the full pipeline over 5 to 10 generator seeds and report mean and spread of the event-level metrics. Without that, threshold 0.40 vs 0.35 and the ablation differences are within noise and you cannot claim either.

items.title: No baseline
items.detail:
- **What's wrong:** there is nothing to show the Random Forest with 228 engineered features beats something simple.
- **Fix:** add at least (a) a per-sensor rolling z-score rule, and (b) an unsupervised model trained on normal data only (IsolationForest). Report them next to the RF. Also be explicit in the README that this is supervised classification on simulated labels; real industrial anomaly data is rarely labeled, which is the main reason people use unsupervised methods.

items.title: Threshold grid is coarse and arbitrary
items.detail:
- **Where:** `model.py:32` (0.30 to 0.70 in 0.05 steps).
- **Fix:** sweep the full precision-recall curve from `metrics.precision_recall_curve` on validation and pick by an explicit rule (max F1, or max recall at precision >= X). Better: select the threshold on the event-level metric from P1-2, since alerts are what get used.

items.title: `/predict` serves a model that no client can realistically call
items.detail:
- **What's wrong:** it expects 228 engineered features computed from up to 78 steps of history. A caller would have to reimplement `features.py` exactly. That is train/serve skew waiting to happen.
- **Fix:** add an endpoint that takes a window of raw readings (at least 79 steps for one machine), runs `build_features` server-side, and scores the last row. Keep the feature endpoint only if you have a reason.

items.title: `sensor_readings.is_anomaly` is always NULL
items.detail:
- **Where:** `db.py` column `is_anomaly`; the raw CSV column is `any_anomaly`. `load_dataframe_to_table` only inserts matching names, so the label is dropped. `timestamp` is also always NULL because the generator never produces one.
- **Evidence:** 50000 rows, 0 non-null `is_anomaly`, 0 non-null `timestamp`.
- **Fix:** rename the column in one place (DB or generator) and add a loader test asserting non-null. Drop `timestamp` or generate it.

items.title: `pipeline_runs` records hardcoded metadata, not what actually ran
items.detail:
- **Where:** `load_to_db.py:31-33` (`fixed_seed=295`, `model_threshold=0.35`, `max_step_gap=3`).
- **Evidence:** the run row says 0.35; the model selected 0.40.
- **Fix:** read the threshold from `artifacts/model_metadata.json`, the seed from the generator output (write it to a small run manifest), and `MAX_STEP_GAP` from `alert_events.py`.

items.title: A load is not atomic
items.detail:
- **Where:** `load_to_db.py:129-160`, `load_dataframe_to_table` commits per table; `load_csv_if_exists` skips missing files with a print.
- **What's wrong:** a missing or failed CSV leaves a run with partial data, and the API serves it as a complete run. `with sqlite3.connect(...)` also does not close the connection; it only manages the transaction.
- **Fix:** one transaction for the whole run; fail (and roll back) if any required file is missing. Close the connection explicitly or use `contextlib.closing`.

items.title: Missing database turns every endpoint into a 500
items.detail:
- **Where:** `db.py:11`. `sqlite3.connect` silently creates an empty file if the path does not exist, then every query fails with "no such table".
- **Evidence:** `GET /runs` with no DB returns 500.
- **Fix:** open read-only from the API (`sqlite3.connect(f"file:{path}?mode=ro", uri=True)`), and return 503 with a clear message from `/health` and other routes if the DB or tables are missing. `/health` should actually check the DB and model artifacts.

items.title: `/predict` reloads the model from disk on every request and leaks internals in errors
items.detail:
- **Where:** `model_serving.py:9` (`joblib.load` inside `predict_feature_row`), `api.py:273-274` (`detail=str(error)`).
- **Evidence:** ~0.24 s per request; error responses expose file paths like `artifacts/model.joblib`.
- **Fix:** load once at startup (FastAPI `lifespan`) and keep it on `app.state`. Log the exception server-side and return a generic message. Store the scikit-learn version in `model_metadata.json` and refuse to load on mismatch, since joblib pickles are not portable across sklearn versions.

items.title: Filters accept any string and silently return nothing
items.detail:
- **Where:** `api.py:113` (`severity: str | None`), sensor and anomaly_type filters. `Literal` is imported and unused.
- **Evidence:** `?severity=critical` returns `[]` instead of 422.
- **Fix:** use `Literal["INFO", "WARNING", "CRITICAL"]` and the sensor/anomaly enums. Return a total count (header or wrapper object) with paginated lists.

items.title: Row alerts are linked to events by re-matching filters, not by ID
items.detail:
- **Where:** `db_queries.py:69-100` (`get_row_alerts_for_event`).
- **Fix:** write `event_id` onto each row alert in `group_alert_events` and store it in `row_alerts`. Then the lookup is a join on `event_id`, and it stops depending on `anomaly_type` (which P0-1 removes anyway).

items.title: Docker images are not self-contained; the hosted deploy config is not in the repo
items.detail:
- **Where:** `.dockerignore` excludes `*.db`, `outputs/`, `artifacts/`; `docker-compose.yml` bind-mounts `.:/app`, which replaces everything the image copied.
- **What's wrong:** locally it works only because of the bind mount. Built and run anywhere else (your Render deploy, per the last three commits), the API has no DB and no model, so every data route 500s and `/predict` 500s. Nothing in the repo describes how the hosted version gets its data.
- **Fix:** pick one: build the data and model inside the image (a build stage that runs the pipeline on the fixed seed), or have the container run the pipeline on startup if the DB is missing. Commit the Render config (`render.yaml`) so the deployment is reproducible. Remove the `.:/app` bind mount from the default compose file (keep it in a `docker-compose.override.yml` for dev). Add a compose `healthcheck` on `/health` and `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`, which also makes the dashboard's polling loop unnecessary locally. Run as a non-root user.

items.title: Dashboard polling and defaults
items.detail:
- **Where:** `dashboard.py:12-27` and `:183-188`.
- **What's wrong:** the comment says ~3 minutes; worst case is 36 x (10 s timeout + 5 s sleep) = 9 minutes of a frozen page. The run picker defaults to run 1, so after reloading data users see the oldest run.
- **Fix:** default to `/runs/latest` (or a selectbox populated from `/runs`). Cap total wait by wall clock, show progress text while waiting, and wrap fetches in `st.cache_data` with a short TTL.

items.title: `MODEL_THRESHOLD` config is dead and misleading
items.detail:
- **Where:** `config.py:8`, `docker-compose.yml` sets `MODEL_THRESHOLD=0.35`. Nothing reads it; the served threshold comes from `model_metadata.json`.
- **Fix:** delete it, or make it an explicit override that `model_serving` honors and logs.

items.title: `model_serving.py` has zero tests.
items.detail: `/predict` is only tested with `predict_feature_row` monkeypatched out (`tests/test_api.py:1695-1705`). The README (`README.md:523`) says tests cover "model inference endpoint"; that is not true. Add a test that trains a tiny model into `tmp_path`, loads it, and checks missing/extra feature handling (after P0-7).

items.title: Feature tests check column names, not values.
items.detail: `tests/test_features.py` would not catch P0-6 or a wrong rolling window. Add hand-computed expectations on a tiny series (e.g. delta, rolling mean, z-score, slope on a known ramp) and the shuffle-invariance test.

items.title: No end-to-end smoke test.
items.detail: Add one test (or CI step) that runs generator (2 machines, ~400 steps) through features, model, alerts, events, `load_to_db`, then hits the API with `TestClient`. This would have caught P0-4 and P2-1.

items.title: Leakage regression tests.
items.detail: Assert that alert construction never reads `target_sensor`/`anomaly_type` (after P0-1), and that no split boundary cuts through an anomaly event (after P1-3).

items.title: `dashboard.py` is untested.
items.detail: Move the fetch/transform code into functions in a separate module and test them; keep Streamlit calls thin. Today all of the page runs at import time.

items.title: 1089 warnings.
items.detail: Fix the `features.py` fragmentation (build feature columns in a dict and `pd.concat(axis=1)` once) and then run pytest with `-W error::FutureWarning` so pandas deprecations fail CI instead of breaking you on the next major version.

items.title: Redundant features.
items.detail: `{sensor}_centered_signal_t` equals `{sensor}_dev` (`features.py:72` vs `:274`); `roll_avg_delta` equals `10_step_diff / 10`; `abs_5_step_diff`/`abs_10_step_diff` are `.abs()` of existing columns; `dir_imbalance_*` is computed and then permanently dropped in `model.py:34`. Remove them. Duplicates split Random Forest importance across copies and make the ablation and importance output misleading.

items.title: `slope` via `rolling().apply(np.polyfit)`
items.detail: (`features.py:14`, `:113-125`) is called ~58k times per 5000 rows. Replace with the closed form (rolling covariance of x and y over rolling variance of x), which is vectorized.

items.title: Dead code and leftovers.
items.detail: `CRITICAL_SCORE_THRESHOLD`, `ALERT_TYPE_THRESHOLD`, `SEVERITY_PRIORITY` in `alerts.py` are unused; `eval_cols` in `alerts.py:32` is unused; `get_alert_events_for_run` and `get_predictions_for_run` in `db_queries.py` are unused by the API; `current_osc_recall`/`voltage_osc_recall` in `model.py:79-80` are debugging leftovers. Replace them with a generic per-type, per-sensor recall table.

items.title: `WARNING_SCORE_THRESHOLD = 0.35`
items.detail: (`alerts.py:157`) is a copy of the old model threshold. With the selected threshold at 0.40 the "low score" template can never fire. Derive score bands from the model threshold in `model_metadata.json`.

items.title: Constants and paths are duplicated across modules.
items.detail: The sensor list is defined in `generator.py`, `features.py`, and `alerts.py`; output paths are hardcoded strings in `generator.py`, `features.py`, `alerts.py`, `alert_events.py`, `evaluate.py`, `load_to_db.py` even though `config.OUTPUT_DIR` exists. Move both into `config.py`.

items.title: `inspect_generator.py` is broken.
items.detail: It imports `matplotlib` (not in requirements), reads `sensor_data_raw.csv` from the repo root (wrong path), and runs at import time. Fix or delete.

items.title: Flat layout.
items.detail: 17 top-level modules. Moving them into a package (`anomaly_detection/`) with a `pyproject.toml` and a CLI entry point would remove the `pythonpath = .` hack in `pytest.ini`. Low priority, but it reads better to anyone reviewing the repo.

items.title: Timestamps.
items.detail: `model.py:284` uses naive `datetime.now()`. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.

items.title: Row-by-row loops.
items.detail: `alerts.build_alerts` and `alert_events.group_alert_events` use `iterrows`. Fine at 2k alerts, but a vectorized version (boolean masks, `groupby` with gap-based `cumsum`) is shorter and easier to test.

items.title: Nothing is pinned
items.detail: (`requirements.txt`). The model artifact is a pickle tied to the scikit-learn version, and the code relies on pandas groupby/rolling index behavior that has changed between majors. Pin exact versions (or use a lock file via `pip-tools`/`uv`), and record the sklearn version in the artifact metadata (P2-5).

items.title: Runtime and dev deps are mixed.
items.detail: `pytest` and `httpx` ship in both Docker images; the API image installs Streamlit and the dashboard image installs scikit-learn. Split into `requirements.txt` (API), `requirements-dashboard.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`.

items.title: Version mismatch.
items.detail: `.python-version`, CI, and Docker use 3.11. CI never tests anything newer. The suite does pass on 3.13 with current pandas 3.0 and scikit-learn 1.9 (I ran it), so adding 3.12 and 3.13 to a CI matrix is cheap.

items.title: CI only runs pytest.
items.detail: Add `ruff` (lint + format check), the end-to-end smoke run from T3, and `pip` caching in `setup-python`. `on: [push, pull_request]` runs twice for every PR push from a branch in the same repo; restrict `push` to `main`.

items.title: The README reports no results.
items.detail: For a portfolio ML project this is the most important missing piece. Add a results table (event-level metrics from P1-2, per-type recall, baseline comparison from P1-7, spread across seeds from P1-6) and a short "limitations" section: simulated data, supervised labels, known label noise.

items.title: Fix the inaccurate claims:
items.detail: the purge gap explanation (`README.md:250`), "missing features are filled with 0" as a feature (`README.md:460`), and "tests cover model inference endpoint" (`README.md:523`).

items.title: Fresh-clone instructions.
items.detail: After P0-4, verify the README steps on a clean clone. Document the deployed version (URL, how it gets data) or remove references to it.

items.title: Explain the design choices
items.detail: that a reviewer will ask about: why a supervised RF, why these thresholds in `SAFETY_THRESHOLDS`, why `MAX_STEP_GAP = 3`, how severity is assigned.

items.detail: Work through this step and note what you can't yet explain. (26)

items.title: Valid answers about code get rejected as a 502
items.detail:
**Verified.** `copilot/providers/openai_answers.py:111` finds citation markers with `re.findall(r"\[(\d+)\]", draft.answer)`. Any answer that mentions indexing, such as `features[0]` or `row[1]`, picks up a fake citation ID and fails the "markers do not match citation IDs" check. I confirmed `"The model reads `features[0]` first [1]."` raises `InvalidGroundedAnswerResponseError`.

**Why it matters:** the corpus is Python source, so answers that quote code are normal. Each one becomes "Grounded answer provider returned an invalid response."

**Fix:** only match markers that are not attached to an identifier or inside backticks (for example a negative lookbehind for `\w`, `]` and `` ` ``), or stop asking the model to write inline markers and render them yourself from `citation_ids`. Add a test with `x[0]` in the answer.

items.title: Request traces are never printed
items.detail:
**Verified.** `copilot/observability.py:136` emits traces with `logger.info` on the `anomalyops.trace` logger, and nothing in `copilot/` or `scripts/` configures a handler or level. Under `uvicorn copilot.api.app:app` I sent two requests and got zero trace lines; only uvicorn's access log appeared. The tests pass because pytest's `caplog` captures INFO on its own.

**Why it matters:** "correlated JSON traces" is a headline feature in the README, and in a real run it produces nothing.

**Fix:** configure the `anomalyops.trace` logger (StreamHandler, INFO, message-only formatter) inside `create_app`, or ship a uvicorn `--log-config` file and document it. Then check the output by running uvicorn, not only through tests.

items.title: Embedding and database failures on `/query` return a generic 500
items.detail:
`copilot/api/app.py` maps grounded-answer errors to 502 but does not catch `EmbeddingProviderError` (OpenAI down, rate limited, bad key) or SQLAlchemy `OperationalError` (Postgres not running). Both fall through to the middleware's `"Internal server error."` at `app.py:125`.

**Why it matters:** the most common failure in pgvector mode (forgot `docker compose up -d postgres`, or a rate limit) gives the least useful message, and it is inconsistent with the 502s you already return for answer failures.

**Fix:** catch `EmbeddingProviderError` and return 502, and catch `OperationalError` and return 503 with "Vector database unavailable." Add one test for each.

items.title: No timeout on OpenAI calls
items.detail:
`copilot/providers/factory.py:65, 108, 150` build `OpenAI(api_key=...)` with SDK defaults, which is a 10-minute timeout with 2 retries. The endpoints are sync, so each stalled call holds a worker thread, and `/triage` can make up to 8 model calls in one request.

**Why it matters:** one slow upstream response can hang a request for many minutes, and the UI just spins.

**Fix:** pass `timeout=30` (or similar) and an explicit `max_retries`, and build one shared client instead of three.

items.title: No upper bounds on request size
items.detail:
**Verified.** `copilot/schemas/query.py:15-16` has `top_k` with only `gt=0` and `query` with only `min_length=1`. `top_k=1000000000` and a 2 MB query both returned 200 in manifest mode. In OpenAI mode, `top_k` sets how many chunks go into the prompt and the query is embedded and sent as is.

**Why it matters:** cost and latency scale with input size, and a typo in a client can send the whole index to the model.

**Fix:** `top_k: int = Field(default=3, gt=0, le=20)` and `query: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=2000)`. `TriageRequest.max_events` already does this (`le=20`), so copy that pattern.

items.title: Manifest mode re-reads and re-embeds the whole corpus on every request
items.detail:
`retrieve_chunks_for_query` (`copilot/api/query_service.py:112`) loads the JSON manifest from disk per request, and `copilot/retrieval/search.py` re-embeds all 133 chunks every time.

**Why it matters:** wasted work that grows linearly with the corpus. Do it together with item 1.

**Fix:** load and index the manifest once in `create_app` and keep it on `app.state`. This also lets a missing manifest fail at startup instead of on the first query.

items.title: Retrieval quality is the real ceiling on the RAG numbers
items.detail:
Your own eval (`evals/results/openai-pgvector-2026-08-06.json`) shows 93% Hit@5 but only 0.67 citation hit rate, 0.67 source recall@5, and 0.71 refusal precision, meaning 2 of 15 answerable questions were refused. Causes I can see in the code:
- `copilot/ingestion/chunking.py` cuts fixed 80-line windows, so functions and README sections are split mid-body.
- Only `chunk.content` is embedded; the file path is not, so "which file handles X" questions lose their best signal.
- Tests make up 58 of 133 chunks. The README's own sample retrieval for a schema question returns three test files and no source file.

**Why it matters:** this is the number a reviewer will quote, and these changes are cheap compared with model changes.

**Fix:** prepend `source_path` to the embedded text, chunk Python on `def`/`class` boundaries and Markdown on headings, and either tag tests as a separate `source_type` or down-rank them. Re-run the semantic eval after each change. Also grow the eval past 20 cases (about 50) before publishing percentages; with 20 cases, one case is 5 points.

items.title: The triage agent fails the whole request on one bad tool call
items.detail:
In `copilot/providers/openai_triage.py`, `_parse_tool_input` (line 185) and the `_execute_*` validators raise `InvalidTriageAgentResponseError` on any malformed tool argument, which ends the request with a 502.

**Why it matters:** models routinely send one bad argument and fix it when told. Right now a single slip costs the user the whole triage.

**Fix:** for tool-argument errors, return the validation message to the model as the tool result and let it retry within `max_tool_rounds`. Keep the strict validation on the final report as it is.

items.title: Reindexing sends every chunk in one embeddings request
items.detail:
`copilot/providers/openai_embeddings.py:90` sends `input=list(texts)` for the whole corpus. The OpenAI embeddings endpoint has per-request limits on input count and total tokens.

**Why it matters:** this works at 133 chunks and breaks once the corpus grows.

**Fix:** batch in groups of about 100 and concatenate the results, keeping your index-order checks.

items.title: Settings: hand-rolled env parsing, duplicated checks, and a fake knob
items.detail:
- `copilot/api/settings.py` parses every env var by hand, and lines 115-119 repeat the integer and positive checks that already ran above them (dead code).
- `pydantic-settings` is a declared dependency but `ApiSettings` is a plain `BaseModel`. Switching to `BaseSettings` with `env_prefix="ANOMALYOPS_"` removes about 90 lines.
- `ANOMALYOPS_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` looks configurable, but the column is hardcoded to `VECTOR(256)` in `copilot/storage/models.py`. Any other value fails at query time. Either remove the setting or check it against the column at startup.

items.title: Dependencies: unused packages and no pins
items.detail:
- `numpy`, `pandas`, `tiktoken`, and `pydantic-settings` are runtime dependencies in `pyproject.toml` but are not imported anywhere in `copilot/` or `scripts/`. They make the Docker image bigger for no benefit.
- Nothing is pinned and there is no lockfile, so CI installs whatever is newest. A FastAPI or `openai` release can turn CI red with no change on your side (it already deprecated `on_event`, see item 13).

**Fix:** remove the unused packages, then add version bounds or a lockfile (`uv lock` or `pip-tools`).

items.title: Replace the deprecated shutdown hook
items.detail: `copilot/api/app.py:284` uses `@app.on_event("shutdown")`, which produces most of the 122 deprecation warnings in the test run. Move it to a `lifespan` handler.

items.title: Small items
items.detail:
- CI tests only Python 3.11 while `pyproject.toml` allows `>=3.11`. I ran the suite on 3.13 and it passes, so adding a 3.12/3.13 matrix costs nothing.
- Typo in a test filename: `tests/test_determinisitc_triage_agent.py`.
- The Dockerfile runs the app as root. Add a non-root `USER`.
- `docker-compose.yml` publishes Postgres on all interfaces with password `anomalyops`. This is fine on a laptop; bind it to `127.0.0.1:5432:5432` anyway so it stays that way.
